evidence.claim: The West Cascades Scenic Byway follows four river systems through forest on the western side of Oregon’s Cascades.

evidence.claim: Breitenbush’s name records a surveyor’s mistaken recollection.
evidence.quote: Minto later gave the man's name to the area, remembering it as "John Breitenbush".

evidence.claim: In 1874, Oregon legislator John Minto led a party looking for a pass over the central Cascades.
evidence.quote: Oregon State legislator John Minto, who, in 1874, led a survey party in search of a pass over Oregon's Central Cascades.

evidence.claim: They encountered a hunter whom Minto remembered as John Breitenbush; people in the Lower Santiam knew him as Lewis Breitenbucher.
evidence.quote: When Minto's maps were published in the 1880s, Lewis Breitenbucher was known to locals in the Lower Santiam, who noted the name Minto used was incorrect.

evidence.claim: The map name became accepted by the end of the nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: the name on Minto's map became the accepted reference toward the end of the 19th century.

evidence.claim: Hot springs later drew visitors along improved trails, roads and bridges.
evidence.quote: By 1901, improvements had been made in the way of trails, roads, and bridges, and a horse pack train operation was running out of Detroit, allowing for an increased number of visitors.

evidence.claim: By 1901, a horse pack train from Detroit served the springs.
evidence.quote: a horse pack train operation was running out of Detroit

evidence.claim: The community’s post office operated from 1928 to 1953, during its development as a hot springs resort.
evidence.quote: In its heyday as a resort, the community was served by a post office, which operated between 1928 and 1953.

evidence.claim: Three Lynx began as Camp 8, a construction settlement built by the Portland Railway, Light and Power Company as early as 1923.
evidence.quote: The town began as a "construction camp" as early as 1923, under the name Camp 8.

evidence.claim: built by the Portland Railway, Light and Power Company
evidence.quote: The settlement was originally built by the Portland Railway, Light and Power Company

evidence.claim: Its first seven cabins, mostly made by the Aladdin Company, became the beginnings of a permanent worker community.
evidence.quote: The town initially had only seven cabins, mostly made by the Aladdin Company. The town soon developed into a permanent worker community.

evidence.claim: Powerhouse modernization reduced the number of workers needed locally, contributing to depopulation.
evidence.quote: One of the main factors for this depopulation was that the company no longer needed as many workers in the area after the powerhouse was modernized

evidence.claim: The school closed in 1988 and was demolished in 2014.
evidence.quote: The school house within the settlement was closed in 1988, and was torn down in 2014.

evidence.claim: In 2018, the company began looking for a successor to take responsibility for the town.
evidence.quote: In 2018, PGE started to consider dropping its involvement in the town and searched for a successor to take care of the town in its place.

evidence.claim: The final permanent residents left in January 2020; the Riverside Fire destroyed most houses that September.
evidence.quote: the final permanent residents left the town in January 2020.

evidence.claim: the Riverside Fire destroyed most houses that September
evidence.quote: on September 8, 2020, the Riverside Fire destroyed most of the houses in the community

evidence.claim: The remaining houses were subsequently demolished.
evidence.quote: the last few houses in the area were completely demolished in 2022
